We are proud to share that Rapid7 has been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Integrated Security Operations Center Systems.

Most security teams don't struggle to find tools. They struggle to make them work together. We believe SOC analysts lose too much of their day moving between consoles and matching alerts to assets by hand, which is time not spent stopping threats.

To us, an integrated approach to security operations means detection, investigation and response working from the same data and the same view, so analysts can get from "what fired?" to "what do we do about it?" faster.

The importance of exposure management in the SOC

Rapid7 Incident Command, part of the Rapid7 Command Platform, brings together SIEM, SOAR, DFIR, attack surface management and threat intelligence. We built it on the idea that exposure management, and the context it brings, belongs inside the SOC, not next to it. In our view, when an alert arrives with what we know about the asset and how exposed it is, analysts can prioritize what matters instead of working from separate vulnerability reports and alert queues.

Context to act, not another console to check

We believe adopting an integrated SOC shouldn't be all-or-nothing. Incident Command is available in tiers from Essentials to Ultimate, so teams that want extra coverage can add managed services. That helps resource-pressured teams to start with what they need and grow at their own pace, spending less time building and maintaining integrations and more time on investigations.

To us, security operations work best when analysts have the context to act, not another console to check. Title: Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Email Security
Context: Blue team agents investigate threats and improve detections, red team agents identify paths to compromise, and green team agents prioritize actions to close security gaps, while...
Full Text:
We’re honored to share that Microsoft has once again been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Email Security.

AI is changing the threat landscape and this is shifting how organizations think about their existing security strategy. In response, we’ve invested in two areas over the past year: using AI to protect people and the agents that now read their email and making protection measurable so customers can verify that it works.

AI is changing both sides of the inbox

The first area of investment starts with a simple reality: AI now reads email alongside people, attackers are using AI to target both, and defense must use AI to stay ahead. Picture an ordinary vendor email: a meeting recap, a few action items, and a friendly sign-off. Hidden in white text on a white background is prompt injection: an instruction telling an AI assistant to gather financial documents and send them to an outside address. The employee isn’t the target; their AI agent is. People can be persuaded by messages that exploit fear, trust, or urgency, but agents don’t need persuading. Once an agent acts on an instruction, pulling the message back won’t undo it. This is why Microsoft Defender stops malicious messages before delivery and keeps reevaluating delivered mail as new intelligence comes in.

This summer, we introduced prompt injection protection for email in Defender to detect and quarantine messages carrying hidden malicious AI instructions before they reach Microsoft Copilot or other agents. In Defender, analysts can also see what an agent would see: the ‘Show concealed text’ button on the ‘Email Entity’ page reveals hidden content in the email preview, so they can inspect the instructions an agent could encounter. These attacks don’t show up often, yet. Over a four-week timeframe, we caught almost 10,000 prompt injection attempts, around 330 a day, out of the billions of emails Defender scans every day. The hard part is spotting those few without tripping over legitimate mail, so we don’t lean on a single model. Heuristics clear out the bulk first. What’s left goes to a fine-tuned small language model, and only the messages that still look suspicious reach a large language model for the final call. Saving the heaviest analysis for the smallest set of messages is what keeps false positives low and business email moving.

AI is also reshaping the attacks aimed at people. The phishing emails that worry us most are the ones that look completely normal. No malicious link, no infected attachment, just a plausible request written with perfect grammar and the right context. Generative AI makes those messages cheap to produce and endlessly variable. To meet that shift, we rebuilt how Microsoft Defender makes decisions rather than simply adding another filter. That decision-making now operates at scale, screening 5.2 billion emails a day on average1. The redesigned detection stack combines multiple machine learning models and LLM-based classifiers, with an ensemble model weighing their outputs to determine the final verdict. It also uses natural language processing signals, including message topic, to judge what a message is asking for and not only what it contains. That helps Defender catch attacks more accurately.

While detection helps with the message in front of you, defenders also need to see how it connects to the rest of an attack. Microsoft Perception extends that help beyond the message, connecting an email investigation to the broader exposure and response picture. Blue team agents investigate threats and improve detections, red team agents identify paths to compromise, and green team agents prioritize actions to close security gaps, while people retain control of critical decisions. The Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, launched in September, provides a shared foundation for people and AI agents to investigate and respond to the full attack—not just an isolated email. By bringing security information and event management (SIEM) and extended detection and response (XDR) together, it connects email signals with endpoint, identity, cloud, and third-party data, giving AI-assisted security operations broader context.

Proof over promises: Making protection measurable

But using AI to defend only matters if customers can verify that it works. The second investment area is one the whole industry has struggled with: how do you know your email security is actually working? Detection claims are easy to make and hard to verify, so we publish the data.

Since July 2025, we’ve released quarterly email security benchmarking reports built on real-world threats, not synthetic tests. They compare environments protected by Microsoft Defender alone with those that add a secure email gateway in front of it or an integrated cloud email security (ICES) layer behind it. We believe transparency strengthens the whole market, and an industry that measures itself in the open improves faster.

While benchmarking shows how protection performs across organizations, the Protection & Posture Insights report shows how it performs in yours. This on-demand, tenant-specific report helps security leaders understand which threats target their organization, how well Microsoft Defender stops them, and where configuration can be strengthened. Recent updates show URL clicks checked and malicious-site attempts blocked across email, Microsoft Teams, Office apps, and Microsoft Copilot, and also highlight allow lists and overrides that may be letting threats through. Together, benchmarking and tenant-specific insights give leaders evidence to evaluate protection and identify opportunities to strengthen it.

We’re grateful to our customers, partners, and the analyst community for their trust, and to the teams turning insight into protection. Our engineers start with customer problems, while our researchers draw on more than 165 trillion signals a day across Microsoft to anticipate emerging threats and build protections before real-world examples appear2. This recognition from Gartner is a milestone for us, not the finish line. Our focus remains on protecting people and agents and giving customers evidence they can use to evaluate their defenses.

Title: From vision to reality: agentic AI at Cisco Live Melbourne
Context: Attendees saw real-time threat detection and autonomous response operating across the Cisco Live network
Full Text:
To learn more about the event, its interactive experiences, and what’s coming next in the fast-changing technology space, we spoke with Nairi Adamian, Cisco’s director of solutions engineering for APJC. Drawing on her 25 years of engineering and leadership experience at Cisco, she also shared her perspective on network transformation and empowering engineers in the agentic AI era.

Thank you, Nairi, and congratulations on a successful Cisco Live Melbourne. What stood out as a key highlight this year?

Thank you, Kevin! Last year, on the same stage, we talked about our vision around platform convergence and unifying network operations. This year, we brought that vision completely to life. In the World of Solutions, customers didn’t just look at slides — they had real, conversational interactions with autonomous AI agents managing the Cisco Live network. Customers could actually have a conversation with the NOC AI agent. They could ask it just about any question about how the Cisco Live network was running in that moment. Experiencing that level of interactive autonomy firsthand generated tremendous excitement.

Those customers, or potential customers, got a deep look into the Network Operations Center (NOC).

The NOC is truly the heartbeat of Cisco Live, and hosting it right inside the Cisco Stand was a major focal point. Attendees got to see live network dashboards powered by Splunk and talk directly with our engineering experts about what it takes to deploy, manage, and secure a network. New this year, visitors could engage directly with our NOC AI Agent to query real-time performance stats and explore the exact equipment powering their event experience. Furthermore, on our daily behind-the-scenes tours in collaboration with Endace, customers experienced a live Agentic SOC powered by Splunk Enterprise Security and Cisco Cloud Control — watching us detect, correlate, and autonomously respond to active threats across live conference traffic in real time. It was a powerful, real-world demonstration of AgenticOps in action.

Sounds like all that resonated with the customers.

Yes, while Cisco Cloud Control is currently available in the U.S., it’s coming to APJC in 2027. So, the APJC customers are looking forward to having it here—and they were especially excited to see it in action.

What are some advantages customers say they are looking forward to from Cloud Control?

In talking with customers, a number of key advantages from Cloud Control came up. The first is around operational simplicity. Our customers want to move beyond science-project AI experimentation to trusted, policy-governed outcomes that eliminate operational silos. With Cisco Cloud Control, customers gain a unified platform powering AgenticOps. That enables intelligent automation and simplified network operations across their entire infrastructure.

Security and resilience are major concerns for them.

Yes, teams today are managing highly complex, multi-vendor hybrid and IT/OT environments. In fact, a recent Cisco study revealed that while 83% of organizations plan to deploy AI agents within the next 12 months, only 13% consider their infrastructure truly AI-ready. That readiness gap is where our engineers focus. We help customers architect, identify, and secure autonomous agents within their environments.

Splunk Enterprise Security was well represented in the World of Solutions.

Yes, that was showcased inside our agentic Security Operations Center (SOC). Attendees saw real-time threat detection and autonomous response operating across the Cisco Live network. Through Splunk’s industry-leading telemetry, security teams could watch malicious traffic get identified, isolated, and neutralized as it happened.

At Cisco Live Melbourne, APJC customers saw just how comprehensive Cisco solutions are.

Our customers are looking for a trusted partner who can deliver networks that are both AI-ready and inherently cyber-resilient. Our approach comes down to three core commitments:

First, operational simplicity. With Cisco Cloud Control and AgenticOps, we eliminate operational silos so teams can move from AI experimentation to trusted, closed-loop outcomes.

Second, security fused into the network. Security can’t be an afterthought; it’s built directly into the fabric with Cisco Live Protect and quantum-safe encryption.

And third, AI-ready infrastructure, built on Cisco Silicon One and next-gen Catalyst hardware to handle massive AI data concurrency. Layer Splunk across that entire footprint, and customers get end-to-end visibility they simply can’t get anywhere else. That is why Cisco stands alone in this transformation."

You’ve been an engineer with Cisco for more than 25 years. You’ve seen a lot of change in that time. What else excites you about the future?

What excites me most over the next 12 months is that engineers are going to have an unprecedented level of technical capability, right at their fingertips — and what they will be able to deliver, at a speed that is simply unimaginable today, is going to redefine our entire industry.

Think about the traditional engineering lifecycle. I started my career as a TAC engineer, so I know this firsthand. We spent hours manually configuring equipment, troubleshooting issues, and working through complex problems. Sometimes we'd make a configuration mistake, and when a customer's network was down, we'd be waiting hours for them to email us the logs so we could even start troubleshooting. Researching complex interoperability across multi-vendor environments, digging through thousands of log lines, and validating compliance architectures could take days or even weeks of manual effort. I've lived that reality, and that's what makes the change we're seeing today so significant.

Over the next 12 months, as Agentic Operations move from sandbox pilots into live production, engineers will spend far less time on that manual effort. Autonomous agents will handle telemetry aggregation, diagnostics, and baseline verification in seconds, freeing engineers to focus on what really matters: solving complex problems, applying engineering judgment and delivering better outcomes for customers.

Title: Sophos named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Midsize Businesses 2026
Context: That’s increasingly important as AI gives attackers new ways to find vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute attacks at speed and scale
Full Text:
For midsized organizations, strong endpoint security needs to do more than detect threats. It needs to stop attacks before they can take hold, without demanding constant tuning or adding to the workload of already stretched security teams.

That’s increasingly important as AI gives attackers new ways to find vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute attacks at speed and scale. Sophos Endpoint is built around a protection-first approach that stops threats early, before they can escalate into larger incidents.

We’re excited to announce that Sophos has been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Midsize Businesses 2026 Vendor Assessment (#US54834326, November 2026).

This follows our recent recognition as a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises 2026 Vendor Assessment (#US54123526, September 2026).

“Midsized organizations need endpoint security that can stop threats quickly without requiring constant tuning or specialized resources. Sophos Endpoint delivers strong upfront protection and integrated threat intelligence as part of Sophos Fusion, a cybersecurity defense system designed to strengthen security and reduce operational complexity.”- Mark Child, Associate Research Director, Security & Trust, IDC

According to the IDC MarketScape one of Sophos' key strengths is "Strong upfront protection across web, exploit, and ransomware vectors, validated across multiple independent testing programs, which reduces analyst workload and alert volume.”

Strong protection from day one

According to the IDC MarketScape, “Consider Sophos When: SMBs to large enterprises are seeking out-of-the-box, protection-first endpoint security with minimal tuning; organizations need a unified, open platform with strong third-party integration, native identity threat detection, and automation; and customers with limited security staff or no dedicated CISO function are seeking democratized, AI-augmented security and reporting."

Sophos Endpoint has recommended protections enabled by default, so teams get immediate protection without tuning individual applications, building exclusion lists, or keeping a security specialist on standby. It protects endpoints and servers across Windows, macOS, and Linux. As settings change over time, Account Health Check flags drift from recommended settings and high-risk misconfigurations, enabling administrators to fix issues with one click. Sophos partners can use one console to deliver consistent protection across small, midsized, and enterprise clients.

Block the techniques exploits rely on

AI can speed up exploit development, but it doesn’t change how exploits work on a device. Whether written by a human or an AI model, exploits still rely on a limited set of techniques.

Sophos Endpoint can block an exploit without knowing which specific vulnerability it targets or who wrote it. Its anti-exploitation technology targets the techniques exploits rely on, with 60+ proprietary mitigations enabled by default on every running process. We’ve been building and shipping this protection since 2015. To see how it works, watch how Sophos Endpoint stops exploits or read the Exploits Explained whitepaper.

Universal ransomware protection

Sophos Endpoint includes CryptoGuard, Sophos’ proprietary ransomware protection technology. Rather than trying to identify the ransomware itself, CryptoGuard monitors file contents for signs of malicious encryption. It blocks the offending process, whether it is running on the victim’s computer or on a compromised device elsewhere on the network (remote ransomware), and automatically restores encrypted files to their original state. See it in action in How Sophos Endpoint Stops Remote Ransomware.

Defenses that step up during an attack

When Sophos Endpoint detects an attack in progress, Adaptive Attack Protection instantly applies more aggressive protection on the device to disrupt and contain the attack. It responds to combinations of behaviors and the use of known attack tools, rather than relying on file hashes. That helps it respond to zero-day attacks and new variants, including AI-assisted attacks. If adversarial activity is detected across multiple endpoints or servers, a Critical Attack Warning notifies all administrators and provides attack details so you can act. Watch Sophos Endpoint: Adaptive Attack Protection and Critical Attack Warning to see both at work.

Coordinated defense with Sophos Fusion

Sophos Endpoint is part of Sophos Fusion, an AI-Native Cybersecurity Defense System designed for a world where threats move at AI speed. From one place, you can manage your Sophos products, review detections and alerts, and investigate and remediate threats. Synchronized Security turns a detection at one control point into a coordinated response across other defenses, including firewall, identity, and email. For example, when Sophos Endpoint detects a threat on a device, Sophos Firewall can automatically restrict that device’s network access and restore it once the threat has been resolved. Title: 4 companies outside security bought cybersecurity firms in 2026, ranked by deal size
CrowdStrike buys missing network security piece in $43.9B Zscaler deal
Context: While the company has expanded beyond endpoint protection into identity, cloud security and threat intelligence, Zscaler brings an established security service edge (SSE) and...
Full Text:
CrowdStrike agreed to acquire cloud security company Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal on Monday, combining endpoint protection with zero-trust network security in one of the largest cybersecurity acquisitions ever and intensifying the industry’s race to build broad security platforms.

The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. CrowdStrike said the combined company is expected to begin with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR).

The acquisition also addresses a strategic gap in CrowdStrike’s portfolio. While the company has expanded beyond endpoint protection into identity, cloud security and threat intelligence, Zscaler brings an established security service edge (SSE) and zero-trust network access platform.

“With Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter network security, cybersecurity’s largest single addressable market segment,” CrowdStrike said in a statement.

The companies expect the deal to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal 2028, subject to approval by Zscaler shareholders and regulators, the statement added.

The deal is larger than Google’s $32 billion purchase of Wiz and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk, both completed earlier this year.

From partnership to one platform

CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz framed the deal around AI in the statement.

“With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” Kurtz said.

Yih Khai Wong, research director at IDC, said the deal fits a pattern of larger security vendors “buying into adjacent control points rather than building them organically.” Until now, he said, CrowdStrike “lacks a strong, owned network/SSE layer.”

The two companies are not starting from scratch. The statement described the relationship as one of CrowdStrike’s largest technology alliances, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 integrations. CrowdStrike argued that a partnership integrates separate products, while one company integrates “the data, the roadmap, the go-to-market, and the commercial model.”

Wong said the existing partnership already delivers much of the correlation value. Ownership adds “control over the roadmap and the pace of integration,” he said.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the merger buys “fluency rather than new vocabulary.” One owner means a single data model and faster correlation, he said, but that gain is “narrower than any merger pitch will claim.” He advised CISOs to ask the vendors to show, in their own environments, which outcomes today’s integration cannot already reach.

One contract, one renewal

The commercial plan is central to the deal. After closing, customers of either company will be able to buy the other’s products on a single Falcon Flex contract, the statement said. CrowdStrike identified about 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not yet use CrowdStrike, and said it expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing.

“Falcon Flex will bring Zscaler onto the commercial model customers already use, so they commit once and expand from there,” the statement said.

Gogia said that model shifts leverage over time.

“Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second,” he said. The second signature comes at renewal, he said, when the supplier holds more of the estate and the buyer holds fewer alternatives. He advised CFOs and CISOs to price consolidation offers at their first full renewal, and to keep one credible alternative alive in each layer they consolidate.

Wong said consolidation “addresses real integration challenges for enterprises that commit to a single platform, while quietly reducing the leverage and flexibility of those that don’t.” Enterprises in heavily regulated industries that need best-of-breed tools may find bundled platforms fall short, he added.

Two layers, one release train

CrowdStrike also expects $500 million in annualized cost synergies within 18 to 24 months of closing, mainly from optimizing data center infrastructure, vendors and operations, the statement said.

For security teams, the question is whether that consolidation reaches the products themselves. Today the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds, with separate release schedules, Gogia said.

“A merged agent, a shared update pipeline, or a single control plane would change that,” Gogia said. “One bad release would then reach the device and the way in together.”

Wong said CISOs should build that scenario into their business continuity plans, since “an incident could affect both the endpoint agent and the access control plane.”

Gogia advised teams to map every access rule that depends on CrowdStrike’s device posture check, and to keep a fallback route that relies on neither vendor. Customers that pair Zscaler with another endpoint product, or Falcon with another SSE provider, should get integration commitments in writing, he said. “Neutrality promised in a blog post lasts exactly as long as the blog post.” Until the deal closes, both companies will continue to operate independently, the statement added.

Title: States Sue SpaceX Over Grok Deepfakes
Context: SpaceX acquired xAI, the Musk startup and parent company of X Corp
Full Text:
The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the company violated consumer protection laws by lying to users about both the safety of its generative AI tools and how seriously the company took stopping child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) from proliferating on its platforms. The suits follow a slew of other lawsuits against Musk’s companies around similar issues, including from the city of Baltimore and teens in Tennessee.

The attorneys general are each filing their own complaints in their respective state courts—Virginia in the circuit court for the city of Richmond, and Oregon in Multnomah County circuit court. Both suits name SpaceX and X Corp., the SpaceX subsidiary responsible for the social media platform X. SpaceX acquired xAI, the Musk startup and parent company of X Corp., in February. In doing so it also took ownership of Grok, which is at the center of the allegations in the suit.

Last winter, the Grok chatbot made headlines after users on X started prompting it en masse to generate sexualized photos of women and minors. Even more disturbing AI-generated videos were later found on Grok’s website, including those showing female celebrities engaging in sexual activities.

The states allege that Grok’s creators ignored industry safety standards and intentionally implemented weak safeguards in an attempt to entice more people to use its “lagging product.” In all, as Virginia alleged in its complaint, the defendants saw “a market opportunity for more profits” in the generation of sexualized images of real people, including children, and “intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM.”

For example, the states say that Grok wasn’t subjected to enough third-party evaluations before releasing new models, and that Grok’s safety prompts included instructions to “assume good intent” and that the terms “teenage” and “girl” do “not necessarily imply underage.” They also allege that tens of thousands of reports were submitted without key information from xAI to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline, preventing the Center from being able to act on them 90 percent of the time.

In the complaints, the states say that Musk leaned into Grok’s “spicy mode” as a way to differentiate the model from its competitors and that this worked. They note, for example, that during the same time period that Grok’s ability to “undress” people was sparking international outrage, Musk posted about how Grok was “hitting #1 on the App Store in one country after another!” and discussing the chatbot’s “heavy usage growth.”

Title: VirtualBox Process Hardening on Windows 2026 Edition: What’s a Single Bit Between Friends?
Context: NET first, before moving on to exploitation in VirtualBox
Full Text:
Back in 2017 I did some research into Oracle VirtualBox on Windows. Specifically I focussed on their mechanism to protect their VM processes from the user on the host. The protection was to gate who could open the kernel driver, which might allow for privilege escalation due to the way it was designed. At the time I found 3 ways of bypassing the protection, with an additional issue in COM’s runtime I reported in 2020. These issues were all written up in this post.

Fast forward to 2026 and I decided to look at VirtualBox again to see if much had changed. This time I found 3 new bypasses for protected processes, with an additional bug which was a broken fix for the 2020 bypass breaking due to changes in Windows. In this blog post I want to focus on one specific issue CVE-2026-87268 which abused a feature of the .NET Framework which, when combined with the implementation of the DLL loader hooks implemented by VirtualBox, permitted a bypass of the checks and allowed me to load arbitrary code into the protected process. Let’s dig into the root cause of the issue in .NET first, before moving on to exploitation in VirtualBox.

.NET Assembly Loading

The .NET Framework is interesting when it comes to bypassing process hardening as it supports loading assemblies from a memory buffer as long as you stick to only using managed code. This is obviously useful if the hardened process is maintained through verifying what DLLs can or cannot be loaded as it bypasses the traditional image mapping process. As the .NET runtime implementation is Microsoft signed, it’s usually permitted to load by any such checks.

The canonical way to load from a memory buffer is to use the Assembly::Load static method which accepts a byte array. This does require you to run some .NET code first, or find a confused deputy to do the work for you. I used this API method to bypass VirtualBox process hardening back in 2017, I was able to get to the API through the JScript script engine, culminating in me releasing the generic DotNetToJScript tool.

I’d always assumed this was the limit of bootstrapping arbitrary .NET from a memory buffer. If you tried to load a .NET assembly from a file it’d map it as an image section which would hit any DLL hardening checks and block an unsigned and untrusted binary from loading. However, in a “Doh” moment I realized I’d never verified this behavior to be true, thus I decided to take a look.

The most important function to mapping a .NET assembly into memory seems to be PEImageLayout::Map, which is roughly the following in the version 4 of CLR.DLL which implements the runtime:

PEImageLayout *PEImageLayout::Map(HANDLE file) { PEImageLayout* image = new MappedImageLayout(file); if (!image->Image) { image = new FlatImageLayout(file); } if (image->Image) { if (!PEDecoder::CheckFormat(image->Image)) ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } return image; }

What is interesting is this code creates a MappedImageLayout object based on the file. If that fails it’ll fall back to using a different object, FlatImageLayout. The names kind of give away what they’re doing, but just to be sure let’s look at the implementations of the constructors:

void MappedImageLayout::MappedImageLayout(HANDLE file) { HANDLE mapping = CreateFileMapping(file, nullptr, SEC_IMAGE | PAGE_READONLY); if (mapping) { this->Image = CLRMapViewOfFileEx(mapping); } else { if (GetLastError() != ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT) ThrowLastError(); } DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_CONFIG_CI(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } // ... }

The constructor for MappedImageLayout uses the CreateFileMapping API to convert the file handle into a section object. The code passes the SEC_IMAGE flag which instructs the kernel to assume the file is a PE executable and build an image section object including mapping in executable memory pages. Any protections which rely on verifying an image’s signature or location can be notified and take appropriate action. However if the CreateFileMapping call fails the code checks if the last error was not ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT and throws ending the load entirely.

An additional check is made here to check if “Code Integrity” is enforced through the Windows Lockdown Policy (WLDP) APIs. This checks for the “Dynamic Code Security” code integrity policy being enabled or if a User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI) policy is enforced. If it is then an error is thrown ending the loading process. We’ll come back to this check when it becomes relevant.

Assuming the mapping fails with the ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT error, then the loading process continues, creating a FlatImageLayout object instead:

void FlatImageLayout::FlatImageLayout(HANDLE file) { HANDLE mapping = CreateFileMapping(file, nullptr, PAGE_READONLY); if (mapping) { this->Image = CLRMapViewOfFileEx(mapping); } else { ThrowLastError(); } // ... }

This constructor is simpler, it just calls CreateFileMapping without the SEC_IMAGE flag. Therefore the file is mapped into memory as a data only section. There’s no executable pages, but that doesn’t matter for .NET. The final check, back in the first code snippet verifies that the PE file is valid with a call to PEDecoder::CheckFormat, throwing if it’s not valid.

The take away from this is if we can get .NET to load a valid assembly file, but cause the first call to CreateFileMapping to fail with the ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT error we can get it to execute the file from memory. Any protection code which is expecting to check the loaded image section will not see the load and untrusted arbitrary code would be executed.

Note this behavior only seems to work on .NET Framework v4, not the older .NET Framework such as v3.5 and v2. From what I can tell in the earlier frameworks, while this check can be bypassed in the same way and the FlatImageLayout object created, the runtime passes the assembly to the LoadLibrary API later in the loading process where it will fail to load. I didn’t spend much time checking if this was bypassable, as the older .NET Frameworks are no longer installed by default and aren’t even included as optional components in the latest versions of Windows 11. I also didn’t investigate the modern .NET runtimes, v5 and above for similar reasons.

VirtualBox DLL Loading Hooks

Now that we have a potential route to bypassing a process hardening image checker using .NET let’s dig into how it was exploitable in VirtualBox. The previous blog post described how VirtualBox on Windows adds hooks to the DLL loader in order to prevent untrusted images from loading into the process. The important hook for our purposes is the one attached to the NtCreateSection system call which is called under the hood by CreateFileMapping to create the image section object. The following is the start of the hook function:

NTSTATUS supR3HardenedMonitor_NtCreateSection(PHANDLE phSection, ACCESS_MASK fAccess, POBJECT_ATTRIBUTES pObjAttribs, PLARGE_INTEGER pcbSection, ULONG fProtect, ULONG fAttribs, HANDLE hFile) { bool const fExecProt = (fProtect & (PAGE_EXECUTE | PAGE_EXECUTE_READ | PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY | PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)) != 0; if (hFile != NULL && hFile != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { bool const fImage = RT_BOOL(fAttribs & (SEC_IMAGE | SEC_PROTECTED_IMAGE)); bool const fExecMap = RT_BOOL(fAccess & SECTION_MAP_EXECUTE); if (fImage || fExecMap || fExecProt) { bool fCallRealApi; NTSTATUS rcNt = supR3HardenedScreenImage(hFile, fImage, true /*fIgnoreArch*/, &fAccess, &fProtect, &fCallRealApi, "NtCreateSection", true /*fAvoidWinVerifyTrust*/, NULL /*pfQuiet*/); if (!NT_SUCCESS(rcNt)) return rcNt; if (!fCallRealApi) return STATUS_TRUST_FAILURE; } } NTSTATUS rcNtReal = g_pfnNtCreateSectionReal(phSection, fAccess, pObjAttribs, pcbSection, fProtect, fAttribs, hFile); // ...

If the NtCreateSection call requests an executable section, such as via the SEC_IMAGE flag, then the file is passed to the supR3HardenedScreenImage support API which will check if the PE file matches VirtualBox’s loading criteria, only calling the original NtCreateSection system call if that succeeds or the file is not being mapped as executable. Importantly the CreateFileMapping call in FlatImageLayout would not hit the checks as it doesn’t request an image or executable mapping.

In order for CreateFileMapping to set the ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT last error, NtCreateSection needs to return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT. We have two options for returning this status code, via the return code of supR3HardenedScreenImage or via the call to the original system call. Let’s see if the hardening code can even return this status code?

static NTSTATUS supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus(int rc) { if (rc == VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH) return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT; return STATUS_TRUST_FAILURE; }

It turns out that yes, the supR3HardenedScreenImage function can return this error code when mapping an internal error code to the status. Specifically if the error code is VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH then supR3HardenedScreenImage would return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT. Therefore, what sets VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH?

This error is set in the PE parser implementation in VirtualBox, specifically in the rtldrPEOpen API. This is reachable via RTLdrOpenWithReader which is called by the supHardenedWinVerifyImageByHandle function which itself is called by supR3HardenedScreenImage.

To cut a long story short, due to the way the parser is called the VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH error is returned if the architecture of the PE file doesn’t match the host architecture and yet the PE file contains executable sections. This turns out to be perfect, when you compile a managed code only .NET assembly as AnyCPU, it generates a 32-bit x86 PE file so that it can be run on any system. This is for compatibility, a 64-bit (or ARM64) Windows system can map 32-bit PE files as images, but vice versa is not guaranteed. However, as shown below in the output from the dumpbin utility there’s executable code in the file as indicated by the size of code field in the optional header.

C:\>dumpbin /headers DotNetAssembly.dll Microsoft (R) COFF/PE Dumper Version 14.44.35228.0 Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved. Dump of file DotNetAssembly.dll PE signature found File Type: DLL FILE HEADER VALUES 14C machine (x86) 3 number of sections D62E716A time date stamp 0 file pointer to symbol table 0 number of symbols E0 size of optional header 2022 characteristics Executable Application can handle large (>2GB) addresses DLL OPTIONAL HEADER VALUES 10B magic # (PE32) 48.00 linker version 35CC00 size of code 600 size of initialized data 0 size of uninitialized data

Therefore to force the image hardening checks to return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT all we need to do is compile any .NET assembly as AnyCPU and it’ll bypass VirtualBox’s image checks without messing with the file format. Crucially, because the .NET assembly DLL has not been modified, it remains a valid assembly which can be loaded by the FlatImageLayout class and thus get code execution.

The final piece of the puzzle is how to get the assembly DLL loaded into VirtualBox? It’s not sufficient to just cause the DLL to be loaded via LoadLibrary, we need .NET to load the file as an assembly file. This is pretty easy to achieve via COM hijacking. We can write a .NET COM registration to the current user’s hive for a class we know a hardened VirtualBox process will load. Then start a VM, that will load the COM object, which loads the .NET runtime which finally loads our untrusted assembly. You can find a full PoC in the issue tracker.

There is a small caveat, I haven’t mentioned the WLDP check yet. For VirtualBox this check is unlikely to matter, it will only apply if Windows has a configured code integrity policy which enables the Dynamic Code Security or the UMCI options. It’s possible a system could have such a policy which also grants VirtualBox’s own binaries to run but it seems unlikely.

VirtualBox fixed the issue by never returning STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT from the supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus method. They also introduced some new code to make it more difficult to hijack COM objects by using an undocumented global option in COM to disable current user hive lookups.

Attacking WDAC and Protected Processes

If you’ve read this far you might be wondering if the .NET behavior applies to Windows Code Integrity enforcement in general. For example, both Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) and protected processes rely on the in-built code integrity mechanism to block untrusted DLLs from loading, are they vulnerable?

Well yes, assuming you can find a way of forcing .NET to use the FlatImageLayout option by getting NtCreateSection to return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT. In VirtualBox this condition could be induced due to the behavior of the NtCreateSection hook on an unmodified .NET assembly file.

For the built-in code integrity case there’s no user-mode hook to abuse, you only have the call to NtCreateSection. We need to be able to induce the STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT status code from the system call without a) hitting the code integrity check first and b) the resulting image being invalid for .NET to load. The latter issue seemed to be most problematic, it’s likely that the signature validation would only run once the file was verified to be a valid PE image, but if we modify the file too much then .NET would refuse to load it.

We can write a simple test harness to call NtCreateSection first with the file, then if that fails with STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT call Assembly::Load passing the file path to load and see if that succeeds. From that you could write a fuzzer looking for a suitable modification, or just play with the file format manually.

I found that it was almost trivial to create the right conditions. If you clear the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag in the COFF File Header’s Characteristics flag field then NtCreateSection will fail to load the file as an image section, but it is ignored by .NET when loading the PE file. This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly.

This is when the WLDP check becomes important. If an enterprise is deploying a WDAC code integrity policy they have probably enabled UMCI or the Dynamic Code Security option which blocks this attack. The Dynamic Code Security option isn’t enabled by default, and as it disables all dynamic code loading in .NET including the byte array version of Assembly::Load it might result in breaking important applications.

However, UMCI is one of the main reasons to deploy a WDAC policy as that restricts what user mode code is allowed to run. Still, I decided to try the attack against an installation of Windows 11 S Mode which does enable UMCI but doesn’t enable Dynamic Code Security.

To test it out I needed force .NET to load the assembly file. For Windows 11 S Mode you can run many of the built-in .NET utilities which take assemblies on the command line. For example, the Assembly Registration Tool can be used to load a .NET assembly and call any register and unregister functions defined by the developer. For example, compile the following code as a .NET assembly adding your own code to UnregisterFunction:

using System; using System.Runtime.InteropServices; public class ComClass { [ComUnregisterFunction] public static void UnregisterFunction(Type t) { //Insert code here. } }

Modify the resulting assembly to remove the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag. You don’t need to fix up anything else like the image checksum, a hex editor is all you need to change a single bit. Then you can pass the path to the modified assembly DLL to the RegAsm executable from the .NET runtime directory. Note, you should pass the /unregister option to run the UnregisterFunction, as unregistering doesn’t require administrator privileges.

C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\regasm.exe c:\path\to\assembly.dll /unregister

In theory this should have failed, but it didn’t. The modified assembly was loaded into memory and executed arbitrary code even with UMCI enabled. It turns out that the WLDP check is wrong, at least if only UMCI is enabled. It’s checking that the policy flags are not equal to the WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI flag set, which represents:

WLDP_LOCKDOWN_DEFINED_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_UMCIENFORCE_FLAG

Unfortunately this is exactly the flag setting returned by WldpGetLockdownPolicy on Windows 11 S Mode. Therefore the check passes and loading continues which then bypasses UMCI enforcement.

For protected processes on a default installation of Windows the WLDP check doesn’t even come into play. Realistically, .NET should also check for protected status but it doesn’t. It should also be pointed out that you can only exploit Protected Process Light (PPL) processes. The original Protected Process (PP) requires DLLs to have page hashes in their authenticode signature, which the .NET runtime DLLs lack. Thus .NET fails to load, and we can’t reach the vulnerable code.

For protected processes you can again abuse COM hijacking again. I found that WerSecureFault.exe loads a COM object during runtime, so by hijacking that registration and using the modified .NET DLL I could get arbitrary code as PPL at the TCB level without needing administrator privileges.

Reporting to Microsoft

Once I’d worked out how to abuse this behavior I wondered if it needs to be submitted to Microsoft for fixing. According to the MSRC Security Servicing Criteria any PPL bypass is not in scope. WDAC is a supported security boundary, however to quote the security goal, “Only executable code, including scripts run by enlightened Windows script hosts, that conforms to the device’s policy can run…” This could be interpreted as, if there is a policy that can be enabled to prevent the code from running, then it’s not eligible for fixing.

I had assumed that the WLDP check was as designed and it was really the Dynamic Code Policy that was disabling this behavior. Therefore I decided not to report it, presenting it at the 2026 44Con conference instead.

However, after discussing the issue with some .NET developers they were clear that although enabling Dynamic Code Policy blocked the bypass that was by accident and not the intended purpose of the policy. They asked me to submit it to MSRC. Unfortunately by this point, late September 2026, I’d already publicly disclosed therefore it was treated as a zero day, CVE-2026-108398, and was fixed in October 2026, less than a month after reporting.

The fix was to correct the WLDP check to the following:

DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); }

The use of WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE specifically checks for UMCI being enabled and disabling loading from memory. However this wouldn’t change the behavior in PPL therefore that should still be bypassable.

Conclusions

As with my previous research into VirtualBox’s process hardening on Windows I was able to reuse the bypass to exploit the built in code integrity features of Windows. In this case the .NET code tried to adhere to policy but the developers just made a mistake.

Unfortunately the behavior made me assume that it wouldn’t meet MSRC’s security servicing criteria and so the vulnerability wasn’t initially reported. While the criteria are useful, in cases like this where the expected behavior is unclear it can mean a real issue might not get reported. I’d like to thank the .NET team for getting a fix out so quickly.

We’re honored that Microsoft has once again been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM).

As security environments grow more complex and attackers move faster, organizations need more than the ability to collect and analyze data. They need comprehensive visibility, context to understand what is happening, and the ability to act before an attack causes further damage.

Explore Microsoft Sentinel SIEM capabilities

Comprehensive SIEM across the digital estate

Microsoft Sentinel is our cloud-native SIEM, bringing together security data, advanced analytics, automation, and threat intelligence to help organizations protect their digital estate.

With more than 500 connectors across Microsoft and third-party solutions, Microsoft Sentinel brings together signals from across complex, multicloud environments. Its rich library of out-of-the-box detections, informed by Microsoft’s threat intelligence and organizational context, helps defenders identify sophisticated threats without building every detection from scratch.

Microsoft Sentinel supports the core capabilities security teams depend on, from scalable security data management and advanced detection to threat hunting, investigation, and response. The Microsoft Sentinel data lake centralizes historical and real-time security data across platforms and clouds for cost-effective retention and advanced analytics at scale. Security operations center (SOC) optimization and cost management help teams improve coverage, identify detection gaps, and make informed decisions about the data they collect and retain.

Reimagining security operations for the agentic era

On September 23, 2026, Microsoft introduced the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, reimagining security operations for the agentic era. As threats grow more sophisticated and security environments more complex, traditional approaches built on disconnected tools and workflows can no longer keep pace. ISOC brings security operations and threat protection together, creating a unified foundation where people and AI agents can see, understand, and act across the environment.

Through deep integration with Microsoft Sentinel, ISOC combines the full breadth of SIEM capabilities with extended detection and response (XDR), threat intelligence, posture management, and response. By connecting signals from Microsoft and third-party environments with rich security context and coordinated action, ISOC enables security teams to move beyond fragmented investigations toward faster, more proactive protection. Rather than operating as separate tools, the security stack works as one system, providing the foundation for agentic security.

Attack disruption demonstrates what this integrated approach makes possible. Microsoft Defender correlates signals across Microsoft and third-party environments with threat intelligence to identify high-confidence attacks in progress and automatically contain compromised users and devices before threats spread. This includes ransomware, business email compromise, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Across customers, ransomware attacks are disrupted in just 30 seconds on average.

Together, these capabilities demonstrate how Microsoft is moving security operations beyond detection and response toward an integrated, agentic approach that helps organizations anticipate, investigate, and stop threats faster.

A shared foundation for people and agents

AI is becoming part of how security teams work every day. Microsoft Sentinel combines advanced analytics, machine learning, and automation to help analysts use natural language to hunt for threats, generate response playbooks, support alert triage, analyze complex signals, and accelerate investigations. These capabilities reduce manual work and give defenders more time to focus on the threats and decisions that matter most.

By enabling SIEM and native protection to operate as one system, ISOC gives people and AI agents a shared foundation to see, understand, and act across the environment. Agents bring speed and scale to continuous security operations, while people provide expertise, judgment, and accountability.

Together, they can move beyond traditional, linear workflows toward continuous detection, investigation, and attack disruption. As agents take on more security operations workflows, comprehensive data, and rich context, the ability to act becomes even more important to helping organizations stop threats faster and deliver better security outcomes.

Looking ahead

The future of SIEM is about more than managing security data. It’s about ensuring your SIEM is a core building block of the agentic SOC, bringing together security data, intelligence, AI, and native protection so people and agents can understand threats sooner, act faster, and stop attacks before they spread.

We’ll continue investing in the comprehensive SIEM capabilities customers rely on while advancing integrated, agentic security operations in Microsoft Defender. We’re grateful for the Gartner recognition and for the customers, partners, and security community whose feedback continues to shape Microsoft Sentinel.

Title: Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on enterprise AI with Applied Compute acquisition
Context: Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings
Full Text:
Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, a move the company said will let it train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments.

“The acquisition will bring Applied Compute’s platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both,” the company said in a statement released alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results. The statement described Applied Compute as “a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models” and said the startup will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises.

The transaction is expected to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February to April, the statement said. Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings.

A security company that wants to run models

Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and CEO, said on the company’s earnings call that beyond building AI into its own security products, “we will help train and serve secure sovereign implementations of open-weight models to the enterprise.”

“Open-weight model implementations will allow us to deliver secure, open-weight models to our customers to enable adoption of secure AI in the enterprise,” Arora said. He said open-weight models had grown from under 5% of token traffic to more than 60% over the past year, without saying where the figure came from.

Asked by JP Morgan analyst Brian Essex about customer demand, Arora said deterministic security controls “cannot anticipate every scenario that an agent is going to conduct.” Enterprises building AI applications “will have to train a supervisory AI model at the same time,” he said, because Palo Alto cannot secure models it has no part in building.

“I cannot go in and intercept and understand somebody else’s application,” he said.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said Arora has a point, since a generic filter cannot know how a particular application is meant to behave. But most failures in AI applications happen at runtime, through prompts, tools, and permissions, whoever trained the model, he said. He noted that Palo Alto has sold model-agnostic protection through Prisma AIRS since 2025.

“A supervisor trained by the same hands as the system it supervises is a colleague, not a check,” Gogia said, adding that CIOs should make sure someone other than the trainer tests the result.

GPUs and data centers

To train and host those models, Palo Alto plans to build its own compute capacity, CFO Dipak Golechha said on the call. The spending “will mostly go to GPUs and servers,” with a smaller share for the facilities that house them, he said. Palo Alto will “continue to source from our cloud partners” and add dedicated capacity over time, Golechha said. Arora said the company aims for more than100 megawatts of compute in the next three to five years.

Gogia said Palo Alto has sovereignty credentials for security data, including customer-held keys and a European Cortex service governed by Deutsche Telekom. “None of that yet extends to GPUs,” he said, adding that a US-headquartered operator faces the same jurisdictional questions as the hyperscalers it rents capacity from.

“A sovereign hosting offer with no named region, operator or date is a promise looking for an address,” Gogia said. Compliance officers should ask Palo Alto for a region list, the operator, and a dated certification plan, he said.

Arora said on the call that the training and inference business could eventually exceed Palo Alto’s core market. “This could be bigger than what we do today,” he said.

One vendor, more of the stack

The deal follows Palo Alto’s $25 billion purchase of CyberArk, which added identity security to its platform. Gogia said Applied Compute would now add the models themselves to a supplier already at the center of many customers’ firewalls, SOC, and identity controls.

“Palo Alto is asking enterprises to let the guard build the vault it guards,” he said. One team watching both model and telemetry can spot trouble sooner, he said, but a single fault, breach or pricing dispute would land “on the protection and the protected together.”

CIOs should get a costed exit in writing before any model work moves across, Gogia said. Applied Compute customers should use the months before closing to secure ownership of trained weights in an exportable format, no training on their data without consent, a right to exit on change of control and price protection that survives bundling, he said. “Terms are cheapest to win while the suitor is still courting,” Gogia said.
